newsitem.title: FRANCE: French palm-tree vote could decide a cliffhanger.
newsitem.headline: French palm-tree vote could decide a cliffhanger.

text.p: If Sunday's general election runoff in metropolitan France ends in a dead heat, the decision on who rules in Paris will come down to votes cast thousands of kilometres (miles) away beneath Caribbean palm trees and in the South American jungle.
Voting in mainland France ends at eight p.m. (1800 gmt) and projected results will be known moments later.
But polling stations will still be open on the balmy French Caribbean islands of Martinique and Guadeloupe and in the steamy South American territory of French Guiana where it will only be afternoon.
Voting will still be under way too in the mist-shrouded North Atlantic islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, off the Canadian coast.
Because of differences in time zones, results from those areas will land in Paris between one and two a.m. on Monday (2300 GMT Sunday and 0000 GMT) -- the last votes to be counted.

In what some will regard as the symbolic redressing of a historical injustice, the one million residents of Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana will thus have the last word on the future of a country which shipped most of their ancestors across the Atlantic as slaves from Africa 300 years ago to cut sugar cane.
The white residents of St. Pierre and Miquelon number fewer than 7,000 and are descendants of Breton and Norman fishermen.

Martinique has four seats in the 577-member French National Assembly and last Sunday's first round of voting indicated one would go to the left, one to the right and the result of the two others was uncertain.
Guadeloupe also has four seats. The left is expected to take three and the right one.
French Guiana's two seats are expected to be split evenly while the seat for Saint-Pierre and Miquelon was expected to go to the right.
Voting in other French overseas areas which are to the east of mainland France and whose time zones are therefore ahead of Paris will have ended by then.
The two seats for French Polynesia in the South Pacific were captured by the right on the first round.
In Reunion Island in the Indian Ocean, the right won one seat and the left won another. Each side expects a further seat while a fifth is uncertain.
The right won one seat in New Caledonia, also in the Pacific, and expects to take the second. The result for the single seat in tiny Wallis and Futuna in the same region is uncertain.
The possibility that voters who have never set foot in Europe will make the difference is a scenario which, though existing theoretically for decades, has never seriously been put to the test.

Of the 22 seats for France's overseas departments and territories, the centre-right held 12 in the outgoing assembly, the left six and independents, who voted either way according to the issue, the final four.
